title: How Habeas Corpus Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain habeas corpus: its Latin meaning ("you have the body"), its origins in English common law in the seventeenth century (tracing back to the Magna Carta), how it works in American practice as a petition after trial and appeals, and its role as a buffer between the state and the individual. They cover the Constitution's suspension clause and historical suspensions: Lincoln during the Civil War, the Japanese American internment in World War Two (not restored until Gerald Ford's 1976 executive order), and the Military Commissions Act of 2006, which stripped habeas rights from enemy combatants, including the case of Maher Arar. They touch on Obama's expected plans to repeal the Act and set up a separate tribunal. The episode ends with listener mail about non-turkey Thanksgiving meals.

segments.title: Opening banter and inauguration
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with small talk about cold weather expected for the January inauguration and Obama's plan to restore habeas corpus, then introduce the term.

segments.title: Meaning and purpose of habeas corpus
segments.summary: The term is Latin for 'you have the body,' a judge's order to a jailer to bring a prisoner in to determine whether imprisonment is legal. It is a mechanism that puts constitutional due process guarantees into action, such as the right to counsel, speedy and fair trial.

segments.title: Origins in English common law
segments.summary: Habeas corpus predates the Framers and developed in English common law in the seventeenth century, after Parliament responded to abuses against Catholics under a Church of England-focused monarchy. Some say its roots lie in the Magna Carta of 1215.

segments.title: How a habeas petition works in American practice
segments.summary: After trial, conviction and appeals, a prisoner can file a habeas petition arguing an unfair trial, such as an inadequate or drunk attorney or hidden exculpatory evidence. The judge decides whether to hold a hearing, not a retrial, and the petition can come in waves when a prosecutor is discredited.

segments.title: Suspension clause and historical suspensions
segments.summary: The Constitution allows suspension only in cases of insurrection or rebellion when public safety requires it. Lincoln suspended it during the Civil War, and it was used against Japanese Americans in World War Two, with restoration only by Gerald Ford's 1976 executive order.

segments.title: Military Commissions Act of 2006
segments.summary: The Act revoked habeas corpus for anyone deemed an enemy combatant, and it was passed after a Supreme Court ruling against Guantanamo detentions. Its retroactive provisions applied back to September 11, 2001, and it allowed torture-derived testimony.

segments.title: Maher Arar case and Obama's planned reforms
segments.summary: A Syrian-born Canadian engineer, Maher Arar, was detained at JFK in 2002, rendered to Syria, and tortured before being released. Obama is expected to repeal the Act, close Guantanamo, and create a secret tribunal for high-value suspects.

segments.title: Listener mail on non-turkey Thanksgiving
segments.summary: Listeners respond to a call for non-vegetarians who skip turkey: one family serves grilled steak and smoked salmon, another eats capon, and a third listener dislikes turkey and has made alternatives. Hosts invite listeners to send feedback and sign off.
